nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What was the main focus of the study conducted by Munyai and colleagues?
nodes.answer: The study focused on assessing the macroinvertebrate community structure in relation to water and sediment chemistry in a subtropical African river system.
nodes.paragraph: Environmental characteristics shape macroinvertebrate community structure across spatiotemporal scales in a subtropical African river system Linton F. Munyai1 , Busisiwe P . Gumede1, Farai Dondofema2 & Tatenda Dalu1 Understanding the impact of human activities and environmental drivers on macroinvertebrate communities is critical to adequately manage river ecosystems under multiple stressors. In this study, we assessed macroinvertebrate community structure in relation to water and sediment chemistry. Samples (i.e., water, sediment and macroinvertebrates) were collected from 16 sites along the subtropical Luvuvhu River (South Africa) mainstem and its tributaries across two seasons (i.e., cool dry (June), hot wet (November)). The analysed data was assessed using multivariate analyses and diversity matrices. Significant differences were observed across seasons and river sections for most water (i.e., pH, temperature, resistivity, ammonium, phosphates) and sediment (i.e., potassium, sodium, copper, zinc, boron, sediment organic carbon) variables. Macroinvertebrates exhibited high diversity during hot wet season compared to the cool dry season, with a six distinct macroinvertebrates families (i.e., Odonata, Diptera, Coleoptera, Hemiptera, Trichoptera, Ephemeroptera) having a high taxon abundances.

nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: What habitats were sampled along the transect?
nodes.answer: The habitats sampled included pools, bedrock, littoral/riparian vegetation/macrophytes, stones in current, stones out of current, rapids/riffles, gravel, sand, and mud.
nodes.paragraph: The following habitats were sampled along a 100 m transect for each sample: pools, bedrock, littoral/riparian vegetation/macrophytes, stones in current, stones out of current and rapids/riffles, gravel, sand and mud for a total time of 8 min. The net was fully immersed in the aquatic environment, and the collection of macroinvertebrates was conducted by systematically sweeping a designated area. The methodology encompassed the act of traversing the water while utilising a sampling net, and employing forceful movements to displace aquatic macrophytes, sand, and boulders. This action was undertaken with the purpose of dislodging macroinvertebrates that might be attached to the mentioned substrates. To avoid the potential escape of active macroinvertebrates, the net was expeditiously retrieved from the water column. The macroinvertebrates were afterwards transferred into a 500 mL plastic container and preserved in 70% ethanol solution. Macroinvertebrates were then taken to the laboratory for identification up to genus and/or species level in most instances following Fry27 identification guides. Data analysis Sediment metal, nutrient concentrations and water environmental variables (with the exception of pH) were log transformed to test for homogeneity of variances and normality.

nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: What challenge is highlighted regarding hydromorphological restoration despite advances in wastewater treatment?
nodes.answer: The challenge is that hydromorphological restoration often falls short of achieving ecological recovery despite substantial advances in water quality.
nodes.paragraph: Ecological Processes (2025) 14:30 It is widely believed that the recovery of benthic inver - tebrate assemblages in Europe has primarily resulted from improvements in water quality (Haase et al. 2023; Sinclair et al. 2024). While water quality enhancements have undoubtedly played a crucial role, the relationship between these improvements and broader ecological out - comes is more complex than it might appear, especially at larger scales. This complexity raises critical questions about additional factors that influence ecological recov - ery. For instance, hydromorphological restoration pro - jects, which aim to restore physical habitat conditions, have shown varying degrees of success (Kail et al. 2015; Lu et al. 2019). While some studies report positive out - comes (e.g., Feld et al. 2018; Li et al. 2018), others find minimal or no improvements beyond the local habitat scale (e.g., Verdonschot et al. 2016; White et al. 2017). This inconsistency highlights a significant challenge: despite substantial advances in wastewater treatment and water quality, hydromorphological restoration often falls short of achieving ecological recovery.

nodes.question: What type of empirical studies support the shifts from abiotic to biotic controls in community structure?
nodes.answer: Empirical studies examining the influence of abiotic and biotic factors on stream macroinvertebrate communities and the role of connectivity and seasonality in stream restoration support these shifts.
nodes.paragraph: According to the ARC, different factors dominate at various stages of recovery. Species tolerance to envi - ronmental stressors plays a critical role during degrada - tion phases, while dispersal constraints shape community composition in the early phases of recovery. As ecosys - items mature, biotic interactions, such as competition with established species, become increasingly important. These shifts from abiotic to biotic controls in commu - nity structure and succession have also been observed in empirical studies, such as those examining the relative influence of abiotic and biotic factors on stream mac - roinvertebrate communities (Toskey et al. 2024) and the role of connectivity and seasonality in shaping succession after stream restoration (Westveer et al. 2018). A recent case study by Gillmann et al. (2024a) on a restored catchment supports this perspective, highlight - ing the importance of species dispersal capacity and increasing interspecific competition during recovery, alongside a decrease in species tolerance to organic pol - lution.
